verdicts.text: In both Pulumi ESC and Vault, secrets can be stored and accessed through a CLI, SDK, or editor interface, and granular access controls can be implemented across all secrets.
verdicts.evidence: On the ESC side this checks out: the Pulumi CLI has `pulumi env`, the public pulumi/esc-sdk repo exists, and ESC has an editor UI. The page's own table also marks "Client SDKs: Yes/Yes" and "Access controls: Yes/Yes". Vault having a CLI, SDKs, a UI and policy-based access controls is widely known, but I didn't check it against a HashiCorp source in this session.
verdicts.source: gh search repos esc-sdk --owner pulumi (pulumi/esc-sdk); repo:content/docs/esc/vs/vault.md L74-82, L147-150
verdicts.framing_note: "Granular access controls ... across all secrets" is broad wording but a normal way to describe ESC's RBAC and Vault's policies.

verdicts.text: Pulumi ESC is fully open source and licensed under Apache License 2.0.
verdicts.evidence: The license part checks out: the GitHub API reports that the pulumi/esc repo is licensed "Apache-2.0". "Fully open source" goes too far, though. That repo is the ESC engine, CLI and SDK, while the ESC service runs on Pulumi Cloud. The same page (L52) calls ESC a "Fully managed SaaS service provided by Pulumi Cloud", and Pulumi Cloud is not open source.
verdicts.source: gh api repos/pulumi/esc --jq .license.spdx_id → Apache-2.0; repo:content/docs/esc/vs/vault.md L52
verdicts.framing_note: overclaim: the pulumi/esc repo (engine/CLI) is Apache-2.0, but the claim widens this to "ESC is fully open source", which includes the hosted Pulumi Cloud service.
verdicts.intuition_flag: "Fully open source" for a service that is only offered as SaaS is a red flag. Suggested wording: "ESC's evaluation engine and CLI are open source (Apache 2.0)".

verdicts.text: Pulumi ESC is fully open source and licensed under Apache 2.0.
verdicts.evidence: The GitHub API shows the pulumi/esc repo license is "Apache-2.0", so the Apache 2.0 part is accurate. But that repo covers the CLI and evaluation engine. The repo describes ESC as "a centralized, secure service", and the same page (L52) calls ESC a "Fully managed SaaS service provided by Pulumi Cloud". The hosted service isn't open source, so "fully open source" claims more than the source shows.
verdicts.source: gh api repos/pulumi/esc --jq .license.spdx_id → Apache-2.0; repo:content/docs/esc/vs/vault.md L27, L46-52
verdicts.framing_note: overclaim — the pulumi/esc repo (CLI/engine) being Apache-2.0 becomes 'ESC is fully open source', even though the Pulumi Cloud service isn't open source
verdicts.intuition_flag: 'Fully open source' clashes with the same page calling ESC a fully managed SaaS in Pulumi Cloud

verdicts.text: Pulumi ESC environments can be composed together from multiple other environments, so shared configuration is inherited rather than duplicated.
verdicts.evidence: The pulumi/esc README says: "Each environment can be composed from multiple environments." It also says: "Composable environments: Environments support importing one into another, allowing for easy composability and inheritance of shared secrets and configuration."

verdicts.text: Pulumi ESC environments can reference secrets stored in Vault, and through ESC those secrets can be organized as collections that are versioned, branched, and composed inside other collections.
verdicts.evidence: The pulumi/esc CLI source includes env_version*.go (versioning, tags, rollback) and env_clone.go (clone/fork, which is roughly what "branching" means here). Composition through imports is core to ESC. I couldn't fetch the Vault provider (vault-secrets) source this session because GitHub rate-limited the requests. The page's own table says ESC supports "pulling and using secrets from multiple sources including HashiCorp Vault", but that's the file under review, so it doesn't count as independent proof.
verdicts.source: gh api repos/pulumi/esc/contents/cmd/esc/cli (env_clone.go, env_version.go, env_version_tag.go, env_version_rollback.go)
verdicts.intuition_flag: "Branched" is loose wording: ESC can clone environments, but it has no git-style branching.

verdicts.text: Vault offers a hosted cloud service and self-hosting, and self-hosting Vault requires significant management overhead.
verdicts.evidence: HashiCorp's docs say "HCP Vault Dedicated is a hosted version of Vault Enterprise operated by Hashicorp on your behalf." Self-hosting is available through Vault Enterprise and Community Edition. On overhead, a HashiCorp blog says self-managed users are "maintaining multiple regional clusters, infrastructure, monitoring systems, and on-call staffing." That supports the claim, though "significant" is a judgment call.
verdicts.framing_note: Both the hosted and self-hosted options are confirmed. The overhead is backed by HashiCorp's own contrast between its managed service and running Vault yourself, but "significant" is qualitative.
verdicts.intuition_flag: HCP Vault Secrets, the lighter hosted option, was retired as of July 2026. The only hosted Vault left is HCP Vault Dedicated, so the doc shouldn't suggest more than one hosted tier.

verdicts.text: Both Pulumi ESC and Vault provide a key-value store.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) HashiCorp's docs say "The kv secrets engine is a generic key-value store used to store arbitrary secrets." Pulumi's ESC guide says "ESC environments store configuration as key-value pairs in YAML under a top-level values key."
verdicts.framing_note: Vault half confirmed by HashiCorp's own docs. ESC half rests on a separate Pulumi docs page (not the reviewed file), which supports but does not prove the claim; confidence set to medium for that reason.

verdicts.text: Pulumi ESC supports pulling and using secrets from multiple sources including HashiCorp Vault, 1Password, AWS Secrets Manager; Vault can only store and manage secrets stored in Vault.
verdicts.evidence: The ESC providers page lists "[1password-secrets] | Import secrets from 1Password", "[aws-secrets] | Import secrets from AWS Secrets Manager", and "[vault-secrets] | Import secrets from HashiCorp Vault", which confirms the ESC half of the claim. The Vault half ("can only store and manage secrets stored in Vault") is competitive framing about a third-party product, and I did not check it against HashiCorp sources.
verdicts.intuition_flag: "Vault can only store and manage secrets stored in Vault" may overstate the limitation. Vault has dynamic secrets engines and Vault Secrets Sync, which pushes secrets out to external stores, though it doesn't pull secrets in from other managers.

verdicts.text: Vault can only store and manage secrets stored in Vault.
verdicts.evidence: HashiCorp describes Vault Enterprise 1.16+ Secrets Sync as "centralizing the governance and control of secrets that are stored within other secret managers" (AWS SM, Azure KV, GCP, GitHub, etc.). Nuance: Vault docs say the sync is one-way with "Vault remains the system of records", so Vault can't pull in or aggregate secrets that already live elsewhere. That means the claim's intent partly holds, but the absolute "can only" wording overstates it.
verdicts.framing_note: Claim is a Pulumi competitive assertion with no cited source; the absolute "only" ignores Secrets Sync (Enterprise) and dynamic secrets engines that manage credentials in external systems.
verdicts.intuition_flag: An absolute "can only" about a competitor's capabilities. Suggest rewording to say Vault must be the system of record and can't import secrets from other stores, and noting that Secrets Sync is Enterprise-only.

verdicts.text: Pulumi ESC supports both a GUI and a Document Editor with autocomplete, docs hover, and error checking.
verdicts.evidence: The only place I found this wording is the page under review (L70: "Yes, supports both GUI and powerful Document Editor with autocomplete, docs hover, and error checking"), and a page can't verify its own claim. The ESC doc paths I guessed don't exist in the repo, and GitHub code search was rate-limited (HTTP 429/403), so I found no independent source for the editor's features.
verdicts.source: read_file content/docs/esc/vs/vault.md (pattern editor|autocomplete|hover); gh search code attempts rate-limited
verdicts.intuition_flag: Sounds right (the ESC console has a table view plus a YAML editor), but I couldn't confirm autocomplete, docs hover, or error checking from any source.

verdicts.text: Vault's editing and authoring support is limited: it offers a key/value form editor with a JSON toggle.
verdicts.evidence: HashiCorp's KV tutorial describes the UI's key/value form plus a JSON toggle: "Instead of entering the key-value pairs one by one, you can enter the secret values using JSON." The KV v2 cookbook also says: "use the JSON toggle to write your key/value data as JSON."
verdicts.framing_note: The factual part (a KV form editor with a JSON toggle) matches HashiCorp's docs exactly. Calling it "limited" is the author's own competitive opinion, not something a source can check.

verdicts.text: Pulumi ESC is available as `pulumi env` in the Pulumi CLI, and supports injecting application secrets as environment variables and modifying secrets.
verdicts.evidence: The auto-generated CLI reference, generated from pulumi/pulumi, documents `pulumi env` as "Manage environments" and links to the ESC project page. Its subcommands include `pulumi env run` ("Open the environment with the given name and run a command"), which injects environment variables, and `pulumi env set`/`edit`/`remove`, which modify values.

verdicts.text: Vault Agent's process supervisor mode can inject secrets as environment variables into a supervised process.
verdicts.evidence: HashiCorp's official Vault docs say: "Vault Agent will inject secrets referenced in the env_template configuration blocks as environment variables into the child process specified in the exec block."
verdicts.framing_note: The docs' "child process specified in the exec block" means the same thing as the claim's "supervised process".

verdicts.text: Both Pulumi ESC and Vault offer client SDKs.
verdicts.evidence: The pulumi/esc-sdk repo exists and publishes Pulumi ESC client SDKs. For Vault, HashiCorp ships an official Go client library (the `github.com/hashicorp/vault/api` package), which is well documented, but I didn't fetch that in this session.
verdicts.source: gh search repos esc-sdk --owner pulumi → pulumi/esc-sdk

verdicts.text: Pulumi ESC supports a declarative provider via the Pulumi Service Provider, which allows management (create, update, delete) of collections of secrets and configuration as a resource through infrastructure as code.
verdicts.evidence: The pulumi-pulumiservice provider has a `Pulumi.PulumiService.Environment` resource that takes an ESC environment definition as YAML (`Organization`, `Project`, `Name`, `Yaml = new StringAsset(yaml)`). It also has related resources: `EnvironmentVersionTag` and `TeamEnvironmentPermission`. Because the environment is a managed IaC resource, create, update and delete work through the normal Pulumi resource lifecycle.
verdicts.framing_note: The claim describes ESC environments as "collections of secrets and configuration". In the provider they are the `Environment` resource, defined by YAML `values`.

verdicts.text: In Pulumi ESC, hierarchical environments inherit values from the environments they import.
verdicts.evidence: The ESC imports docs say: "The values from the imported environments are merged into the current environment using a JSON Merge Patch, with the current values overwriting the imported environment's values where keys are redefined." They also say imports let you "organize configuration hierarchically." Values inherited through imports can be overridden locally.
verdicts.framing_note: Only true for explicit imports, which merge by default. `merge: false` imports and implicit imports don't merge the whole environment. That fits the claim's general framing.

verdicts.text: Vault has no equivalent concept of composable environments; secrets are organized by path convention and the structure is maintained by hand.
verdicts.evidence: HashiCorp's own validated design says "Vault static secrets are organized and accessed using paths", and its secrets-engine docs describe paths behaving like a virtual filesystem. No Vault doc found describes composing or importing one secret set into another the way ESC environments work. The "no equivalent" part is an absence claim, so it rests on a lack of counter-evidence rather than on a direct statement.
verdicts.framing_note: The source confirms path-based organization; "no composable environments" is inferred because no such feature is documented.
verdicts.intuition_flag: "Structure is maintained by hand" is a competitive overstatement: Vault paths, mounts and policies are commonly codified with Terraform or the Vault API. Consider softening it to "by convention".

verdicts.text: In Vault, secrets are individually versioned, which is a limited form of versioning.
verdicts.evidence: HashiCorp's docs confirm versioning is per key: "When running v2 of the kv secrets engine, a key can retain a configurable number of versions," and max_versions is "the number of versions to keep per key." KV v1 has no versioning at all. The word "limited" is Pulumi's own opinion and can't be checked.
verdicts.framing_note: Per-secret versioning only applies to the KV v2 engine. KV v1 and dynamic secrets engines don't version secrets this way, so a blanket "In Vault" is a slight generalization.
verdicts.intuition_flag: "Limited form of versioning" is a competitor-comparison opinion, not a fact that can be checked. Consider saying "KV v2" to be precise.

verdicts.text: In Pulumi ESC, values can be secret or plaintext; in Vault, values can only be secrets.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) Vault's docs say all stored values are encrypted and don't offer a plaintext value type. The KV v1 docs state "only the values set on keys are" encrypted, and the barrier "ensures that only encrypted data is written out." The ESC half (secret via fn::secret, or plaintext) is well-established ESC behavior; this search didn't separately confirm it.
verdicts.framing_note: Vault encrypts every stored value and has no secret/plaintext distinction, which supports the claim that "values can only be secrets." Path and key names are not encrypted, but those aren't values.

verdicts.text: Pulumi ESC allows seeing existing secrets, whereas Vault does not.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) HashiCorp's docs show that Vault lets you read and view existing secrets through the CLI (`vault kv get`), the API, and the UI. The "Read data" page tells UI users to "Click the eye icon to view the desired key value," and the `kv get` page says it "retrieves the value from KV secrets engine at the given key name."
verdicts.intuition_flag: A secrets manager that can't show you your existing secrets is implausible. The comparison row (L104-106) probably means something narrower, like "import/sync existing secrets from other stores," and should be reworded to say that.

verdicts.text: In Pulumi ESC, environments can import secrets from another environment, and secrets updated in the referenced environment automatically propagate to downstream environments.
verdicts.evidence: The ESC imports docs say environments can import "configuration and secrets from other environments" and that "The `imports` key is a list of environments that are resolved at runtime." Because imports resolve at open time, changes made in the imported environment show up downstream. One caveat: imports pinned to a version tag or revision won't pick up those changes.
verdicts.framing_note: The docs say imports are "resolved at runtime," so propagation follows from that. The docs never actually use the word "propagate," and the claim leaves out that version-pinned imports won't update.

verdicts.text: Vault has no first-class environment to reference, so secrets are read by path and Vault has no equivalent secret-referencing concept.
verdicts.evidence: Vault docs describe everything in terms of mounts and paths, e.g. "The read command reads data from Vault at the given path", and "Secrets engines are enabled at a path in Vault." They mention no named, composable environment object. The claim that Vault has "no equivalent" is a negative, so no source can confirm it outright.
verdicts.framing_note: The docs show reads happen by path. That no environment or secret-referencing concept exists is inferred from its absence, not stated anywhere.
verdicts.intuition_flag: Vault Agent/consul-template templates and Vault namespaces do let you reference secrets by path. A reviewer could reasonably say "no equivalent" goes too far.

verdicts.text: Pulumi ESC supports constructing new dynamic values through string interpolation, and Vault does not support interpolating values from other values.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) The ESC docs say you can "use string interpolation to transform values or compose new values from other values." On the Vault side, an open feature request (hashicorp/vault#18337) asks for "secrets that are a 'pointer' / 'link' to another secret", which suggests Vault's storage can't natively reference or interpolate values from other secrets.
verdicts.source: https://www.pulumi.com/docs/esc/environments/working-with-environments/ ; https://github.com/hashicorp/vault/issues/18337 ; WebSearch ran query "HashiCorp Vault secret value interpolation reference other secrets"
verdicts.intuition_flag: Vault's negative is backed only by a feature request and a forum question, not by official docs. Vault Agent/consul-template can build values from several secrets on the client side, so "does not support" holds for Vault's server/KV storage but may be too absolute overall.

verdicts.text: In Pulumi ESC, environments can be forked for testing without rewriting entire environments and overriding specific values; Vault does not support branching or personal configs.
verdicts.evidence: The ESC CLI includes an environment clone command (pulumi/esc cmd/esc/cli/env_clone.go), so environments can be copied for testing. ESC imports let one environment build on another and override specific values instead of rewriting the whole thing. I didn't check the Vault half ("no branching or personal configs") against a Vault source.
verdicts.framing_note: ESC has no feature literally called "fork". The claim loosely combines two real capabilities: clone and import-based overrides.
verdicts.intuition_flag: "Forked" isn't ESC's own term (ESC calls it clone). The Vault "No" is a competitor claim I didn't check.

verdicts.text: `pulumi env diff` shows the changes between two environments or two versions of a single environment; Vault has no equivalent for comparing secrets across environments.
verdicts.evidence: The ESC source (env_diff.go) defines the `diff` subcommand: "Show changes between versions ... This command displays the changes between two environments or two versions of a single environment." `pulumi env` uses this same ESC command set. I didn't check the Vault half (that Vault has no equivalent) against Vault docs. Vault is known to have no built-in secret diff command, so that half is plausible.
verdicts.framing_note: The ESC half matches the command's Long help text word for word. The Vault negative is a claim about a competitor and wasn't checked against Vault sources.
verdicts.intuition_flag: The claim that Vault has 'no equivalent' is a claim about a competitor. Vault KV v2 keeps secret versions, so a reviewer may want to soften the wording.

verdicts.text: Pulumi ESC supports built-in functions such as `toJSON`, `fromJSON`, `fromBase64`, and `toString`, which allow data manipulation for any scenario.
verdicts.evidence: I couldn't confirm this from source this session: GitHub code search hit its rate limit, and the listing of pulumi/esc/eval returned only file names, not the function definitions. Pulumi ESC does have the builtins fn::toJSON, fn::fromJSON, fn::fromBase64 and fn::toString, but that comes from background knowledge, not a passage I fetched.
verdicts.source: gh api repos/pulumi/esc/contents/eval (file listing only); gh search code blocked with HTTP 403 rate limit
verdicts.intuition_flag: "allows data manipulation for any scenario" is marketing overstatement. The claim should drop "any scenario", and a reviewer should check the four function names against the ESC builtin-functions reference.

verdicts.text: Vault provides templating and transformation functions, such as username templating and the Transform secrets engine, rather than functions for composing configuration values.
verdicts.evidence: HashiCorp docs confirm that username templating exists: it is "used in some secret engines to allow operators to define how dynamic usernames are generated." The Transform secrets engine is a real Vault feature, though it is Enterprise-only (ADP); I'm relying on known product facts for that, since it wasn't in this search's results. The contrast in "rather than functions for composing configuration values" is a judgment call. Vault Agent templates and VSO secret transformation templates can compose values from secrets, so this part is only loosely supported.
verdicts.framing_note: Vault docs confirm both named features exist. The comparison with composing configuration values is the author's own characterization.
verdicts.intuition_flag: Vault Agent templates and the VSO 'Secret data transformation' feature (Go templates that build values like connection URLs) arguably do compose configuration values. The Transform engine is Enterprise-only.

verdicts.text: Both Pulumi ESC and Vault provide audit logs.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1 after exhausting its 12-turn cap) HashiCorp's Vault docs say "Audit devices are mountable devices that log requests and responses in Vault." The pulumi/esc README says "All actions taken on environments, secrets, or configuration values are fully logged for auditing."
verdicts.framing_note: Vault turns auditing off by default on new clusters, so it has to be enabled. Pulumi Cloud audit logs may only be available on some paid tiers. Neither point contradicts "both provide audit logs."

verdicts.text: Pulumi ESC uses TLS for encryption in transit and unique encryption keys per environment for encryption at rest.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) Public ESC docs confirm secrets are "encrypted at rest and masked in plaintext output" (pulumi.com/docs/esc/concepts/environments/), but no public page I found confirms TLS in transit or a unique encryption key per environment. That part is about how Pulumi Cloud/ESC itself works, so product source should be checked.
verdicts.source: WebSearch ran query "Pulumi ESC encryption at rest unique key per environment TLS"; https://www.pulumi.com/docs/esc/concepts/environments/
verdicts.intuition_flag: "Unique encryption keys per environment" is a specific key-management claim that the docs I found don't back up. ESC may use per-org or BYOK keys instead, so check this against the pulumi/esc or service source.

verdicts.text: Vault uses a security barrier for all requests made to the backend, which automatically encrypts all data leaving Vault using a 256-bit AES cipher in Galois Counter Mode (GCM) with 96-bit nonces.
verdicts.evidence: HashiCorp's Vault Security Model page says: "Vault uses a security barrier for all requests made to the backend." It also says the barrier encrypts "all data leaving Vault using a 256-bit Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) cipher in the Galois Counter Mode (GCM) with 96-bit nonces." Vault's source (barrier_aes_gcm.go) agrees: it uses a 12-byte nonce and a 256-bit key.
verdicts.framing_note: The claim repeats the source's two sentences almost word for word; the only change is "Advanced Encryption Standard (AES)" shortened to "AES".

verdicts.text: Both Pulumi ESC and Vault provide access controls.
verdicts.evidence: The pricing page (a separate file from the one under review) lists RBAC in Pulumi Cloud: "The Pro edition offers more sophisticated organization management facilities, including RBAC for advanced policy controls." Vault's access policies are a well-known core feature, and the page's own intro also says so, though that intro can't count as evidence. The claim is a generic, low-risk capability statement.

verdicts.text: Vault cloud secrets engines generate short-lived credentials for AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud, and each engine is configured with a static credential that Vault uses to mint them.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) It's true that Vault's AWS, Azure and Google Cloud secrets engines generate short-lived credentials. But the claim that each engine is configured with a static credential is wrong: HashiCorp's AWS API docs say "Credentials can be configured either with IAM access keys for a privileged AWS account, or using Plugin Workload Identity Federation (WIF)". The Google Cloud and Azure engines support the same WIF option, which needs no static secret. The AWS engine can also pick up credentials from the IAM/ECS instance through the SDK.
verdicts.framing_note: "Each engine is configured with a static credential" is stated as always true. HashiCorp documents WIF as a way to avoid static credentials (the AWS and GCP docs mark it Enterprise). A more accurate wording would be "typically configured with a static credential (or WIF in Vault Enterprise)".

verdicts.text: Pulumi Cloud can be used as an OIDC provider from the Pulumi SDK, CLI, UI, and `pulumi-service` provider.
verdicts.evidence: pulumi/pulumi-pulumiservice has OIDC-related examples (`examples/cs-oidc-issuer`, `examples_oidc_preview_test.go`), so the provider does handle OIDC configuration, and Pulumi Cloud/ESC does issue OIDC tokens for dynamic cloud credentials (L153). But the OidcIssuer resource registers outside issuers that Pulumi Cloud trusts, which is not Pulumi Cloud acting as the OIDC provider. I also couldn't confirm the SDK and UI parts of the claim because GitHub code search hit a rate limit.
verdicts.intuition_flag: The claim may mix up two things: Pulumi Cloud as an OIDC provider that issues tokens, and Pulumi Cloud trusting outside issuers (the pulumi-service OidcIssuer resource). Also, a Vault comparison saying Vault's OIDC provider setup is 'only available from the CLI' looks doubtful, since Vault also exposes it through its API and Terraform.

verdicts.text: Configuring Vault as an OIDC provider is only available from the CLI.
verdicts.evidence: HashiCorp's OIDC identity provider docs say "The Vault OIDC provider feature has a full HTTP API." That means configuration isn't limited to the CLI; it can also be done through the API and tools built on it, such as Terraform. I also recall a Vault UI for OIDC provider setup (Access > OIDC Provider, around Vault 1.11+), but I didn't find a page confirming that in this session.
verdicts.intuition_flag: "Only available from the CLI" is unlikely for a Vault feature. Every Vault CLI command wraps the HTTP API, and newer Vault versions ship an OIDC Provider section in the web UI.
